readerTitle: Why the right sales channel depends on what you sell
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (중소상점 대상 기장 서비스, 창고용 컨베이어 제조사) + 가상 적용 (병원용 일정관리 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 좋은 채널은 따로 없다. 채널은 고객 한 명을 얻는 비용과 고객이 구매를 결정하는 방식이 내가 파는 것과 맞을 때만 작동한다.
misconception: 고객이 많이 모이거나 비용이 싼 채널이 가장 좋은 채널이다.

sources.text: 마케팅·영업의 일반 원리: 가격과 구매 복잡도가 높을수록 사람이 개입하는 채널이 필요하다 (셀프서비스, 내부 영업, 현장 영업의 구분)
모든 수치와 기업은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 기장 서비스 계산: 영업 담당자 월 비용 $6,000 ÷ 월 4곳 계약 = 고객당 $1,500. 고객 한 곳의 생애 이익 $1,000(가정) − $1,500 = 고객당 −$500. 모든 수치는 가상입니다.
컨베이어 시스템 약 $80,000, 병원 소프트웨어 연 $60,000 계약은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 업계 가격을 주장하지 않도록 카드 문장에 'around', 'typical'로만 표현했습니다.

cards.title: Two good businesses, two wrong channels
body: A bookkeeping firm hired a salesperson to visit local shops. A machine maker put its machines in an online catalog and ran ads to it.
Both had solid products. Both picked a way of selling that could never work for them, and they failed in opposite directions.

image.label: A salesperson at a small shop door and a giant machine stuck in a website cart
image.brief: 화면을 좌우로 나눔. 왼쪽: 정장 차림 영업 담당자가 작은 가게 문 앞에서 서류 가방을 들고 서 있음. 오른쪽: 거대한 산업용 컨베이어가 웹사이트 장바구니 아이콘에 끼어 있음. 밝은 3D 클레이 스타일. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: How should a $150-a-month service find clients?
body: You run a bookkeeping service for small shops and charge $150 a month. Over the time a typical client stays, you earn about $1,000 in profit from them.
You want to grow faster. Where do you put your money?

options.text: Hire a sales rep to visit shops in person
options.feedback: Visits build trust fast, but a rep is expensive. If each signed client costs more than the $1,000 they bring in, every win loses money.

options.text: Run local online ads to a simple sign-up page, with a short call to answer questions
options.feedback: Cheap per client and close to how shop owners already shop for small services. You lose the personal touch of a visit, but the math works.

options.text: Rent a booth at a big national trade show
options.feedback: You'd meet many owners in a day, but booths are costly and most visitors aren't local shops you can serve. Worth a small test, not a big bet.

cards.title: The rep was good. The channel wasn't.
body: The rep signed clients steadily. But a $150-a-month service can't pay for a person to win each client face to face.

cards.title: Now the opposite mistake.
body: A manufacturer builds custom conveyor systems for warehouses, around $80,000 each. To cut sales costs, it listed them in an online industrial catalog and ran ads.
Traffic came. Serious buyers didn't. A system like this needs an engineer to measure the floor, and the plant manager, finance and safety staff all have to agree.
The catalog was cheap, but it couldn't carry a sale that big and that risky.

image.label: Warehouse buyers around an engineer with a floor plan
image.brief: 창고 바닥에서 엔지니어가 도면을 펼치고, 공장장·재무 담당·안전 담당 세 사람이 둘러서서 보는 장면. 구석에 노트북 화면 속 온라인 카탈로그가 외면당한 채 놓여 있음. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Channel fit
body: **Channel fit** means the way you reach and sell to customers matches what you sell. It has two tests.
*The money test:* what the channel spends to win one customer must be clearly less than that customer is worth to you.

*The buying test:* the channel must match how customers actually decide. A quick, low-risk purchase needs little friction. A big, risky one needs people, proof and time. The bookkeeper failed the money test. The machine maker failed the buying test.

cards.title: A rough ladder of channels
body: As price and complexity rise, the sale usually needs more human help.
list: **Low price, simple:** shelves, self-serve websites, sign-up pages
**Mid price, some questions:** phone or video sales, short demos
**High price, many decision makers:** field sales, site visits, pilots, engineers
cards.callout: Cheap products need cheap channels. Complex products need channels that can explain.
cards.softwareNote: A $20-a-month tool lives on free trials and self-serve sign-up. A $100,000 contract needs a sales team. The same pitch through the wrong channel either costs too much or never closes.

cards.title: Fit isn't fixed.
body: One business can need two channels. The conveyor maker could sell spare parts online and full systems through engineers.
Fit also shifts. If a product gets simpler or its price changes, the right channel can move up or down the ladder.
And early numbers are guesses. Test a channel small before you build a team around it.

cards.title: Now it's hospital software.
body: You sell staff-scheduling software to hospitals. A typical contract is $60,000 a year, and IT, nursing leaders and finance must all sign off.
Your board suggests selling only through a free trial and online checkout, to cut sales costs. What do you do?

options.text: Agree: free trial and online checkout only
options.feedback: Cheap per customer, but few hospitals buy a system that touches every shift from a checkout page. A trial alone won't get IT and finance on board.

options.text: Keep a sales team with demos and a one-ward pilot, and use the trial to let nurse managers try it
options.feedback: It costs more per deal, but a $60,000 contract can carry that cost. The trial still helps, as a tool inside the sales process.

options.text: Shift the budget to social media ads aimed at nurses
options.feedback: Nurses may love the product, but they can't sign the contract. Good for awareness, weak as your main channel.

cards.title: Match the channel to the sale.
body: Before choosing a channel, check two things: what it costs to win one customer there, and whether it fits how your customers decide.
**Try it today:** estimate what one new customer is worth to you. Then estimate what your main channel spends to win one. Is the gap wide enough?
